summary: This Experimental document describes another way to apply the Alternate-Marking Method, a technique for measuring packet loss and delay, to Segment Routing over IPv6. It carries the marking in an experimental TLV in the Segment Routing Header, so it should be used only between cooperating parties in a controlled domain. It may scale or simplify better than the approach in RFC 9343.

eli5.summary: Packets get a colored sticker that switches color now and then, so helpers along the road can count how many were lost or slowed.

subtitle: An experimental way to carry packet-loss and delay markings inside the Segment Routing Header instead of IPv6 option headers.

tldr.problem: The Alternate-Marking Method measures packet loss and delay on live traffic, but it needs a marking field. RFC 9343 puts that field in IPv6 option headers, which some SRv6 nodes may not handle well.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines the AltMark TLV, which carries the same marking fields inside the Segment Routing Header (SRH) of an SRv6 packet, plus optional extended fields such as a timestamp and a sequence number.
tldr.outcome: It is an Independent Submission Experimental alternative to RFC 9343 with no IETF consensus, meant to be run only inside a controlled domain to find out whether the SRH approach is worth adopting.

today: RFC 9947 is an Experimental, Independent Submission published in March 2026. It is not obsoleted or updated by another RFC, and it has no IETF consensus; the standard-track alternative it is compared with is RFC 9343.

sections.title: Why Another Way to Mark Packets
sections.content:
The Alternate-Marking Method (RFC 9341 and RFC 9342) is a passive way to measure packet loss, latency and jitter on live traffic. It works by marking consecutive batches of packets, and it needs a marking field so that flows can be told apart. RFC 9343 defines that field as a TLV in the IPv6 Hop-by-Hop or Destination Options header.

This document instead puts the field in a new TLV in the Segment Routing Header (SRH) of an SRv6 packet. The idea is to take advantage of SR nodes being expected to parse the SRH quickly, while they may not handle Destination Options properly.

This protocol extension was developed outside the IETF as an alternative to the Standards Track RFC 9343 and does not have IETF consensus. It is published to guide experimental implementation and interoperability.

The two approaches can coexist: this document does not change or invalidate any procedure in RFC 9343. The difference shows up when the path between two segment endpoints has several hops. A Hop-by-Hop option is processed at every hop, while the SRH TLV (or a Destination Option placed before the SRH) is processed only at segment endpoints.
sections.eli5: There was already a way to stick the color label on the outside of the parcel. This RFC tries a second way, inside the delivery instructions, to see which works better.

sections.title: The AltMark SRH TLV
sections.content:
The TLV starts with an SRH TLV Type and an SRH TLV Len, then carries the base Alternate-Marking data. The type is taken from the range 124-126, an Experimental code point for a TLV that does not change en route, so everyone taking part must agree on the value used. The length is 6 when no extended fields are present.

  • FlowMonID: a 20-bit unsigned integer identifying the monitored flow, as defined in RFC 9343.
  • L and D: the Loss and Delay flags, the actual alternating marks.
  • NH: says whether extended fields follow. 0x0 means none, and 0x9 means the extended fields are present. The other values are reserved.

Reserved bits MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt. The FlowMonID is needed because the IPv6 Flow Label cannot be used. Because a 20-bit ID set at domain entry can collide even when chosen pseudorandomly, extra flow information can be carried in the extended fields to disambiguate.
sections.eli5: The label has a few boxes: one for the flow's name tag, two for the color stickers, and one that says whether there is extra information stuck on behind it.

sections.title: Optional Extended Fields
sections.content:
When NH is 0x9, the TLV carries Enhanced Alternate Marking fields. These start with a FlowMonID Ext (20 bits, to reduce collisions) and four flags: M (0 for segment-by-segment monitoring, 1 for end-to-end), F (marks fragments so that only one packet is counted), W (flow direction, used when backward monitoring should be set up automatically) and R (reserved, MUST be zero). A Len field gives the size of the extended fields in multiples of 4 bytes.

A 16-bit MetaInfo bitmap says which optional metadata follows, in the order the bits are set. Three bits are defined: a 6-byte timestamp, control information for setting up backward-direction monitoring, and a 4-byte sequence number. The timestamp lets intermediate nodes compare it with their local time and measure one-way delay. The sequence number can detect out-of-order packets in addition to supporting loss measurement.
sections.eli5: If you want more detail, you can attach extra notes behind the label: a clock reading, a note about the way back, or a ticket number to spot parcels that arrive out of order.

sections.title: How Nodes Use the TLV
sections.content:
The measurement domain is the same as the SR controlled domain, and each kind of node has its own job.

  • Ingress SR node: adds the AltMark TLV to the SRH when it encapsulates the packet.
  • Intermediate SR node: a node that cannot process the TLV ignores it, following RFC 8754. A node that can process it checks for it and handles it.
  • Egress SR node: the last node in the segment list, which processes the TLV the same way as the intermediate nodes.

The use of the TLV may be combined with SRv6 network programming (RFC 8986): whether an endpoint processes or ignores the TLV may depend on the SID function of the SID in the destination address. This also lets operators collect marking data only from supporting segment endpoints.

If both the SRH TLV and a Destination Option carry marking data, they coexist without problems, but the information is duplicated. Duplication should be avoided, and analyzing the use of only the SRH TLV is recommended as part of the experiment.
sections.eli5: The first helper sticks the label on, helpers in the middle read it if they know how and ignore it if they do not, and the last helper reads it too.

sections.title: The Experiment
sections.content:
The experiment must use a code point from the Experimental range, and participants should let operators configure the value so that several experiments can run in one network without clashing. It aims to find out whether the SRH TLV brings advantages, especially for implementations that cannot support multiple IPv6 extension headers in one packet, do not support Destination Options processing, or process them on the slow path.

Researchers are invited to compare the SRH AltMark TLV with RFC 9343 on four questions: whether it survives across a network better or worse than an extension header, how its processing performance compares with the Destination Option, whether forwarding performance differs across device architectures, and how the extended fields compare with other on-path telemetry methods. It is expected to stay inside a single service provider network, and initial results are expected within two years of publication.
sections.eli5: It is a science fair test: try the new label spot and see if it is faster, safer or easier than the old one.

sections.title: Security and Controlled Domains
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 9343 apply here too. The fundamental requirement is that Alternate Marking MUST only be applied in a limited domain, which for SRv6 is an SR domain (RFC 8402). The experiment MUST only be deployed within that controlled domain.

Operators need to secure the domain against malicious configuration and attacks, including packets injected into it. The nodes are locally administered, and packets containing the AltMark TLV are prevented from entering or leaving the domain. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: This label is only meant for one trusted neighborhood. Strangers' parcels with fake labels must be kept out, and your labelled parcels must not leave.

fields.name: SRH TLV Type
fields.desc: Experimental code point from the range 124-126.

fields.name: SRH TLV Len
fields.desc: Length of the data fields in bytes; 6 without extended fields.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: FlowMonID
fields.desc: Flow Monitoring Identification, as in RFC 9343.

fields.name: NH
fields.desc: 0x0 no extended fields; 0x9 extended fields present.

items.label: Timestamp
items.desc: A 6-byte timestamp: 16 bits of seconds and 32 bits of nanoseconds.

items.label: Backward-flow control
items.desc: Control information to set up backward-direction flow monitoring.

items.label: Sequence Number
items.desc: A 4-byte sequence number for detecting out-of-order packets.
